**The air is essentially dead calm — there is no detectable wind at all.** Every free-hanging, wind-sensitive object visible in the shot stays exactly plumb and motionless for the entire 87 seconds, and the dust/haze suspended in the air just hangs there instead of being carried away. The stillness is genuine ambient stillness, not the result of shelter or of competing artificial air currents (see point 6 below).

## The scene

A night-time, open-air cultural performance — a Tamil dance-drama, with Tamil lettering on the proscenium signboard and a caparisoned elephant on stage — staged in the outer courtyard of a South Indian temple, whose floodlit gopuram towers rise behind the stage. A green box-truss "goalpost" rig spans the stage carrying moving-head beam lights, and a flown line-array speaker cluster hangs from each truss tower. A large audience is seated in the open in front of the stage. The camera is handheld and drifts and slowly zooms throughout, which has to be removed before anything can be said about what is or isn't moving.

## Evidence

**1. The hoist chain hanging from the lighting truss is perfectly plumb and does not sway — measured.**
On the right-hand truss tower a long steel chain hangs freely from the overhead truss down to a bracket on the hall wall, with the loose tail of chain and cable dangling below it. I tracked this chain by sub-pixel normalised cross-correlation over a continuous 35-second stretch (t ≈ 20–55 s) and simultaneously tracked a rigid patch of the temple building as a reference. Over that period the camera itself moved about 29 px horizontally and 33 px vertically, and the chain followed it with a correlation of 0.995. **The chain's position relative to the rigid building varied by only 0.5 px (standard deviation), 2.4 px peak-to-peak.** Scaling from the box-truss tower beside it (a standard 300–400 mm section spans about 69 px there), one pixel is roughly 5–8 mm, so the chain's entire lateral excursion over those 35 seconds is on the order of a centimetre or less — within measurement noise, and indistinguishable from perfectly still. A multi-metre free-hanging chain is a sensitive pendulum; the lightest real breeze would visibly set it swinging.

**2. The same chain is plumb at every point in the clip, not just in that window.**
Sampling frames at t = 5, 20, 40, 60 and 78 s and cropping tightly around the chain each time shows it as a dead-straight vertical line in all of them, with no tilt and no change in its position relative to the truss leg and the wall behind it.

**3. The hanging temple decorations (thoranam) hang exactly vertical throughout.**

Neither the bodies nor the light frills — which weigh almost nothing — ever tilt, swing or flutter.

**4. Loose cables and safety loops dangle slack and motionless.**
The coils of cable hanging from the wall junction box beside the chain, the cable tails below the hoist, and the loops of safety wire hanging off the flown speaker cabinets all hang limp and unmoving. Light, freely suspended cable responds to weaker air movement than a steel chain does, and none of it stirs.

**5. The drapery is demonstrably still — measured against a rigid control.**
Tracking the same 35-second window: the large white side drape moved by only 0.7 px (sd) horizontally relative to the building, and the pleated red backdrop curtain by 0.4 px. For comparison, a second patch of rigid, immovable masonry tracked against the first gave a residual of 1.8 px — so **both fabrics moved less than the frame-to-frame noise floor of the measurement on known-rigid objects.** Visually, the white drape, the red backdrop and the pink skirt round the stage front keep identical folds at t = 20 and t = 50; nothing lifts, ripples or billows, including the stage-front skirt, which faces straight out into the open courtyard and would be the first thing to move.

So the fans are stationary, and the motionless drapery cannot be explained away as fans counteracting a breeze — there is simply no air movement, indoors or out.

**7. The airborne haze is stagnant: the light beams stay clean, even and persistent.**
The beams are strongly visible as sharp shafts against the night sky for the whole clip, which means a substantial load of dust/haze is suspended in the air above the crowd. Along each trace the brightness is even and continuous: no knots of denser haze travelling through the beam, no dark gaps sweeping along it, no billowing plumes or rolling eddies, and no moment where a beam is scoured clear and then re-fills. Dust kicked up by a crowd this size just sits in the air for the full 87 seconds instead of being flushed away — the signature of non-ventilating, stagnant air. A tall, slender box-truss tower has been erected in the open carrying flown line-array speaker cabinets and a loaded lighting truss, with no visible guy lines and no substantial ballast, and lightweight decorations have been hung from it. # What can be determined about wind at this event

## Setting and what was examined
The clip runs about 87 s at roughly 30 fps, has no audio track, and shows an outdoor, night-time classical-dance performance on an open-fronted stage at a South Indian temple site (a temple tower is visible behind the stage and the stage sign is in Tamil). A green lighting truss with moving-head beams stands in front of the stage and a large crowd watches. Wind can only be judged from objects that respond to moving air. The usable indicators in the frame are: two cylindrical fabric hangings ("thombai") with orange fringes hanging side by side from the left stage pillar, a similar fully visible hanging plus a partly hidden one on the right stage pillar, a chain and loose cable tails hanging from the right truss tower, a sheer white curtain at the back-left of the stage, the visible light beams (which reveal haze in the air), and the crowd. The camera itself drifts and rotates slightly (up to about 40 px over the clip), so all measurements were made relative to fixed features (stage sign, speaker stack, truss towers) and the tilt of each hanging was measured within the object itself, which is unaffected by camera translation.

## Conclusion
There was a light, intermittent breeze (gusty light air, not a steady or strong wind), blowing at least partly from the left of the frame toward the right across the stage front. It was strong enough to swing one light fabric decoration through roughly 8-15 degrees peak to peak and to hold it leaning about 8-12 degrees for several seconds during the strongest gust, but too weak to visibly disturb anything heavier: the paired hangings on the left pillar, the chain and cables on the truss, the curtain, the haze in the light beams and the crowd all remain essentially still. Rough physical reasoning (a light fabric cylinder leaning about 8-12 degrees) puts the gust at only a few metres per second, on the order of Beaufort force 1-2.

## Evidence
1. The fully visible hanging on the right pillar swings like a pendulum. Frame-by-frame tracking of its fringe relative to its top cap shows a smooth oscillation with a period of about 2.4-2.5 s (autocorrelation peak at 2.42 s), consistent with a free-hanging object about 1.5-2 m long. In a slit-scan (kymograph) of the fringe row, the orange fringe traces a clean zig-zag wave while the taut chain and the green truss beside it stay perfectly straight, which confirms the motion is real and not camera shake.
2. The swing amplitude comes and goes in bursts, which is the signature of gusts rather than steady wind. The hanging swings strongly at about 17-30 s, 36-41 s, 58-72 s and 75-85 s (peak-to-peak roughly 8-15 degrees) and is nearly still at about 30-36 s and 42-50 s (tilt standard deviation under about 1 degree, only a few degrees peak to peak).
3. The strongest gust occurs at about 51-60 s. Starting around 51 s the hanging leans progressively with its lower end displaced toward the right of the frame (toward the truss tower and chain), holds a sustained lean of roughly 8-12 degrees (the fringe displaced about 17-20 px over a cap-to-fringe height of about 124 px) from about 54 to 58 s, and returns to vertical by about 60-61 s. In camera-compensated crops it hangs vertical at 52 s, is clearly slanted at 55-58 s and is vertical again at 59-62 s. A sustained one-sided lean needs a steady push for several seconds, which only moving air can supply; sound or structural vibration cannot hold an object off vertical.
4. The two hangings on the left pillar barely move. Their tilt changes by only about 1-2 px (under about 1-2 degrees) over the whole clip, though they show a slight lean in the same direction (lower ends to the right) at about 50-56 s, coinciding with the strongest lean of the right-pillar hanging. They hang closer together, are linked by a small trident ornament and appear more sheltered, so their much smaller response shows the air movement is weak and probably strongest on the right side of the stage front.
5. Direction: every measurable lean displaces the lower ends of the hangings toward the right of the frame, so the air moves from frame-left toward frame-right, roughly along the stage front. Any component toward or away from the camera cannot be judged from this viewpoint.
6. Heavier hanging items are unaffected. The chain from the right truss tower and the loose cable tails below its clamp remain straight in the kymographs apart from slow camera drift, with no sway at 54-58 s.
7. The sheer white curtain at the back-left of the stage is essentially still. Kymographs through its folds show straight, unchanging fold lines for the whole clip; the only changes occur when a stagehand walks in front of it at about 18-20 s and 31-38 s. There is no billowing or flapping. The curtain is inside the hall, so this mainly shows the interior air is calm.
8. Artificial airflow is ruled out as the cause of the swinging. The ceiling fans inside the stage hall are not spinning (blade positions are identical across consecutive frames at about 30.3-30.6 s, with no motion blur), and no pedestal fans are visible anywhere on stage. The stage-front lantern is an electric prop, not a flame, so no flame indicator exists.
9. Secondary indicators are consistent with light air only. The moving-head beams are visible because of haze, and that haze stays uniform with steady, sharp-edged beams rather than streaming sideways or clearing. No flags, banners, bunting, smoke plumes or foliage are in view, and nothing in the crowd (clothing, hair) shows any wind disturbance.

## Summary statement
The determinable facts are: (a) air was moving, because a free-hanging fabric decoration on the right pillar swings repeatedly and leans for several seconds; (b) the movement was intermittent and gusty, because the swing amplitude rises and falls in bursts separated by near-still intervals; (c) it was light, because only the lightest free-hanging object responds while the paired hangings, chain, cables, curtain, haze and crowd do not; and (d) at least a component of it blew from frame-left to frame-right across the stage front. There is no evidence of strong or sustained wind at this event.

The video is a single wide handheld shot, 87 s long, of an outdoor night dance performance on a lit stage facing a seated crowd, with a temple tower behind. ## Conclusion

There is wind, but it is light and gusty, not strong or sustained.

Most of the time the air at stage level is near calm: fabric hangings hang vertically and still. At intervals there are brief gusts strong enough to visibly deflect and flutter a hanging decoration, then die away. Nothing indicates a sustained breeze or high wind.

## Clear evidence

1. **A free-hanging fabric decoration on the stage-right pillar is pushed sideways in brief episodes.** On the white pillar at the right side of the stage opening, just left of the green-lit lighting truss, hangs a long cylindrical patterned fabric decoration with an orange tassel fringe at the bottom. Its top is fixed; its bottom is free.

   - At most times — for example around 2, 10, 18, 26, 34, 42, 50, 60, 62, 64, 72, 74, 78, and 86 s — it hangs straight down with the fringe pointing down.
   - Around 58 s it is caught tilted diagonally, bottom displaced toward the right side of the frame, toward the truss.
   - From about 66 to 70 s it does so again and more clearly: at about 66 s the fringe kicks up sideways to the right; at about 68 s the whole cylinder leans roughly 10–15 degrees from vertical with the bottom toward the truss; by about 72–74 s it has fallen back to vertical. Dense 4–6 fps crops show vertical, then kicked, then vertical again within one to two seconds.

   The pillar, the wall emblem behind the hanging, and the truss do not move between these frames, while the hanging changes angle and the fringe blurs and flips. That rules out camera shake, which would move the background equally. Only moving air, i.e. a gust, lifts and displaces a hanging this way and then lets it fall back.

2. **The gust direction is consistent.** Both the ~58 s and ~66–70 s deflections push the bottom of the hanging toward the same side: the right side of the image, toward the lighting truss. In image terms the gust component at that corner blows along the stage front from the stage-center side toward the stage-right side. No compass direction can be given from this one camera view, and no speed in m/s can be measured, but the relative direction is repeatable.

3. **It is gusty, not continuous.** The hanging returns to vertical for many seconds between events, and frames one to two seconds before and after each kick are vertical. The pair of similar cylindrical hangings on the stage-left pillar, tucked under the roof overhang, stay essentially vertical even during the 62–74 s episode. White drapery at the stage-left side of the interior and the red rear curtain hang in soft vertical folds throughout and never billow, stream, flap, or snap. The dancers' loose costumes move only with dancing, and the audience sits undisturbed. A steady or strong wind would lean the hangings continuously, stir the larger curtains, and disturb clothing. The observed pattern — long still periods plus second-scale kicks of one exposed tassel — means light, intermittent gusts or eddies at the exposed stage-right corner, with sheltered spots staying still.

## What cannot be determined

Wind speed in meters per second, compass direction, and wind above roof height cannot be determined. The spotlight beams sweeping the dark sky change angle because the fixtures pan; their motion is not air motion, and the haze in the beams shows no measurable drift. The ceiling fans turning inside the covered stage area are mechanical and are not wind evidence. The generally limp curtains and vertical hangings put an upper bound — no strong or sustained wind — but the exact lull speed cannot be quantified from video alone.
